utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I'll be very brief. Turns out that Mr. Robinson and I both noticed that in the pace of business yesterday 65 ter number 30953, which was raised in connection with the redirect examination of Mr. Franken, was not tendered and so we would do so now with no objection, as I understand it, from the Defence. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, thank you for the reminder. That will be admitted. Of course, it should have been marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI P4254, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: As indicated by the registrar, we will be sitting until 4.20 today without having to interpose this witness. The first session will be until 10.40, after which we will have a 40-minutes' break, and after which we will sit from 11.20 to 1.00, and then we'll have a two-hours, ten minutes' break, and then we'll sit from 10 past 3.00 to 20 past 4.00. I think that's sufficient time to cover this witness and even we can start -- but we'll see. Mr. Karadzic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Excellencies. Good morning, Your Excellencies. Good morning to all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Tucker. I would like us to go through what you noted personally and what you perceived personally. I would like to draw your attention to a meeting or, rather, what you call the attack in Sarajevo on the 1st of October, 1992. You thought that that was done with the intention of cutting Sarajevo in half, and you said that that was the last such attempt. That's what you said yesterday. Did you know that politically that was not any plan? That was originally the plan of the Yugoslav People's Army that wanted to link its barracks, Marsal Tito and hospital, with the territory of Lukavica, rather, free territory.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not have any knowledge of the kind you describe. All I saw was the -- the attack taking place and the reports which were made by the various UN organisations in Sarajevo, and the deduction that I drew yesterday was General Morillon's supposition. What you describe, I'm not in a position to comment on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I see. Thank you. So that was General Morillon's assumption. It was not rock-hard evidence; right?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The rock-hard evidence was the fact that an attack took place. We obviously did not have access to the plans of the Bosnian Serb Army, and so therefore obviously I cannot confirm one way or the other. What I described was what General Morillon's deductions were from the attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The fact that the other witness testified otherwise does not mean that this witness should agree with him. Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, I don't think, furthermore, that Dr. Karadzic's comment as to what the witness said is appropriate given that the witness testified in closed session, and I'd like to ask for a redaction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. That's how you are wasting your time. As I told you yesterday, please consult Mr. Robinson how to conduct your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Excellency. It's two minutes that were lost, not a lot of time, but the problem is that the amalgamated statement, it doesn't say that this was an assessment. It's presented like evidence. My concern is what kind of attention will be paid to impressions by the Trial Chamber, what the Trial Chamber will do with impressions and generalised statements. But I'll try to have that corrected.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. You confirm then that I was in Geneva and that was also a basis for General Morillon to believe that this was not an attack that had been approved by the political powers; right?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. General Morillon was surprised. Was surprised that an attack took place while diplomatic negotiations were going on in Geneva.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When speaking of March 1993, you speak about the meeting in Belgrade in relation to the crisis that had to do with Srebrenica -- or, rather, the Drina River Valley; right?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Further on, you say that during that time I was in New York and that the general view was that I could not do much from there; right?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the -- the view held by General Morillon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. There is an observation of yours here. You say that you thought that General Mladic was rather independent and that in actual fact he would have taken over if the Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina were in jeopardy. Many of your observations are correct, not to say brilliant, but do you know that this stems from our system itself? For example, do you know that our constitution --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I wanted to -- but did you want the reference for that statement?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Absolutely, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Was the amalgamated statement, paragraph 282 and 277. And the one that had to do with my stay in New York is associated Exhibit 65 ter 08616.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then are you satisfied, Ms. Edgerton?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, not as to the accuracy of Dr. Karadzic's assertion that Mr. Tucker wrote in his amalgamated statement that Dr. Karadzic could not do much from New York, but I'm satisfied with the reference. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That position of Mr. Tucker's is in 08616, the associate exhibit, paragraph 6 of that particular document. The rest is in the amalgamated statement. You wrote in your diary in relation to the 13th of March, 1993 -- actually, could we please have this displayed, 65 ter -- actually, 1D4849. The last page of this document. The fourth one. Could you please read item 4 to us, please.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Commander believes Serb military are going far beyond the direction given by their politicians."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know that in our country the Law on the Organisation of the Army, operative and tactical command over the army was delegated to the Main Staff from the president?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that that was the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is that then in line with your position that you presented in the amalgamated statement, in paragraph 279, about this lack of influence with regard to military issues? Please look at that paragraph 279. Is that in line with the fact that the president does not deal with operative and tactical command?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The understanding -- or rather, the belief that we developed, General Morillon and the staff developed, while I was in Bosnia was that you, Dr. Karadzic, were the president and Commander-in-Chief of the Bosnian Serb armed forces and that General Mladic was the general commanding the Bosnian Serb armed forces. In most cases, we believed that General Mladic and the Bosnian Serb armed forces would do what you directed them to do and what the Serb Assembly directed them to do. However, we believe that if General Mladic believed that they were being ordered to do something or ordered not to do something which was -- which would endanger Bosnian Serbs, that we saw occasions when he, in our view, did not do necessarily what he was ordered to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That is why I wanted to ask you whether your observations -- actually, whether you would have been assisted had you known that in our system, for instance, it was forbidden for politicians to accept capitulation. The constitution said that everyone had to fight to the very last, and from that point of view even the JNA did not need any kind of order to discipline Slovenia. They could have done that without any order coming from the Presidency of Yugoslavia. Did you know these specific characteristics of Tito's constitution?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That I did not, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Then we had this meeting on the 20th of November, 1992, at the Panorama Hotel. So I would like us to highlight a few matters that you observed there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, the pages we saw right now were not included in your exhibit, associate exhibit, and that will be added to the previous diary, or shall we admit it separately? Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, I think we should admit them separately. We have some other excerpts also that are coming in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. That portion of diary will be admitted as a separate Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may make a brief submission in regard to the diary that was just displayed, that single page that was just displayed, and you may -- Your Honour, I think it would be of assistance for the Trial Chamber to have the entry for 13 March 1993 in full rather than just one page out of context.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, 1D4849 is of four pages. Is it not sufficient?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Correct. I didn't realise that Your Honours were dealing with the four pages in total rather than just the one page that was displayed. I wanted to make sure you had the four --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So if we are to admit -- I'm sorry. I was overlapping. If we were to admit four pages, you would have no problem.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Of course not. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. It will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D2026, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 66 of your amalgamated statement, you deal with this meeting and the points that were considered there; right? Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That in this paragraph you deal with our meeting, that is to say, General Morillon's meeting with me that you also attended on the 20th of November, 1992.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and other paragraphs around that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now let us see what your diary says in relation to that meeting. Let us look at 1D6481 then.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's 4681.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: I think I -- I thought I said that, but in ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please read this out to us -- or, rather, interpret for us what it says under item 2. Lower. Below item 2. Yes. Precisely. [In English] "Unfortunately ..."

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Made a lot of efforts to get Serbs to understand and trust UN." Next paragraph: "Unfortunately, have very strong evidence that UNPROFOR is helping other side. Often find Argentinian, Nepalese ammunition with Croatian and Muslim soldiers, NATO food. Yesterday a report that UNPROFOR helped Muslim and Croat soldiers enter Karlovac Cazinska Krajina in a UN convoy," I can't read the last one, and then the last one is, "Have captured Muslim and Croats who said UN smuggled people in UN vehicles and that UNPROFOR attitude is against Serbs." And that is my handwritten notes of what you, Dr. Karadzic, said at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And what about this page that we have on the screen now? Can we see the portion where you said that I had said that it would be very important to establish who started the attacks? Can you confirm that? Can you take a look at that paragraph? That I asked to have it established who it was that started attacks so that we could know who should be held responsible for the shooting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That seems to be the line with the asterisk in the lower.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "Karadzic said it's important to establish accurately who started," and by that he meant started shooting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On that same page could you please indicate to us whether you wrote down that small individual groups are the ones committing crimes and that we are trying to eradicate them.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can the bottom of that page be enlarged? Yes. "Dr. Karadzic stated all sides make atrocities. Serb military are under unified and effective command. Atrocities are committed by small individual groups who we disown and are trying to root out."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we look at page 48 now. That would be the next page. Did you note here that we were not committing ethnic cleansing? Can we see that part on this page 48, that we are not committing ethnic cleansing? I would like to see how much of that you wrote down.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it's the third paragraph down from the top.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. Could you read this for us, please.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Karadzic said that the world needs to be told that the Serb authorities are not ethnic cleansing, et cetera. The war will not end until same pressure is on all sides. We need a balanced approach." Can I see to left, because there's a line going to the left off the screen to me. See whether that leads to a comment. Does it go any further? No. Thank you. And that is what I wrote down that you, Dr. Karadzic, said at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that the partiality and one-sidedness of world media encouraged the Muslims to hope for a military intervention and made them disinterested in peace as much as the Serb side was interested?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I ask a question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: By all means, Mr. Tucker.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Should I answer Dr. Karadzic's question, as I don't see that it is relevant to -- to my evidence here?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You can answer that way, yes. I think that to be an answer, a legitimate one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Well, it is predicated that you agree that the -- there was partiality and one-sidedness, which you may or may not do.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah. The impression -- the belief that I had was that there was impartiality by world media who were focusing on the atrocities and ethnic cleansing being carried out by the Bosnian Serbs in Bosnia. I won't refer at all to the Croatian war, as I was not involved in that. But that was because there was cause to be concerned because of the horrific things that Dr. Karadzic, the forces under your command and under your authority, had been conducting. So, yes, there was partiality, but if your forces had not carried out extraordinary horrific actions, perhaps things would have been more balanced.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But the point is precisely, Mr. Tucker, first of all that we believe that the things that were done by independent elements were ascribed to our army. Secondly, things that the Serb side did were exaggerated while what the other sides committed was ignored, and the actual committing was not established. There was just an impression that was being created. So what was required was to have a more balanced relationship and not to encourage the other side by attacking the Serbs in the media.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Bosnian Serb forces conducted ethnic cleansing to the south-west of Banja Luka. The Bosnian Serb forces under your command carried out the attack on -- on Sarajevo that we discussed earlier. The Bosnian Serb forces continued ethnic cleansing and attacking the -- the enclaves in the east.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Sir. Sir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. -- no, no --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is not an answer to my question. That is not an answer to my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please do not interrupt the witness answering the question. You hear him out and then you can ask another question. Yes. Please continue, Mr. Tucker.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And there is documentary evidence of orders made by the Bosnian Serb Army to conduct these attacks in the eastern enclaves. So I do not accept your -- your premise that all the attacks are done by the Bosnian Serb side were actually small elements out of control.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tucker, with all due respect, if you say that and if you establish that, then this whole proceedings and the Trial Chamber is unnecessary. What I'm asking you is what you established and what you knew. Now we're dealing with your diary, but let me not put any more questions to you. You believe that I was not right when I said that the media should not be encouraging the other side. This is something that we're going to discuss with someone else then. But can you please look at what you said on page 40 -- 48, page 48, about what I said about it being necessary to let the people go out of Sarajevo so that they could survive more easily in the villages? Did you know that since World War II until our civil war, the population of Sarajevo increased nine fold and that the majority of those citizens had their villages, their property, and their homes within the vicinity of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: What am I supposed to be looking at?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So do not make argument. Let's find the passage and put the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [In English] Karadzic said that the best help would be to rebase people from Sarajevo to the villages. [Interpretation] Do you see that part? Where I was making the recommendations for people to be allowed to leave in order to survive more easily?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only see at the bottom a statement by General Morillon about freedom of movement. I cannot see anything by Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Just before this part where you said [In English] "Best help would be to rebase --"

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right. Can you enlarge the screen there. Can you enlarge just above where -- no, below that. Just below where it says "For demilitarisation of Sarajevo." Yes. What Dr. Karadzic said was best help would be to release people from Sarajevo to survive the winter in the villages where they have food, et cetera. That is indeed what Dr. Karadzic said not only at that occasion but a number of other occasions as well. The issue was that from the Bosnian Serb Presidency side, they equated releasing people from Sarajevo to ethnic cleansing forced by military arms.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tucker, were you aware of our position declared even before the war and then reiterated on the 22nd of April in my platform and everywhere at all conferences that the territorial question or the issue of the population would not be prejudiced and that everybody would have the right to return to their hearths once the foundations for a cease-fire were established? Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not aware of details of negotiations prior to my arrival in Bosnia in October 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tucker, I would like to dispute in their entirety the assertions on ethnic cleansing, the relocation of the population and taking of territory, military action. All that means nothing, because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's an argument.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: -- did you establish that? Was that something that you knew? No, no, no. Mr. Tucker, if you are drawing conclusions then you are required to know the elements, and the element that I am talking about is that we said that no military capture is going to have any effect or be prejudicial on the return of the civilians. How can we talk about ethnic cleansing when the civilians would be able to return? Not the civilians but the population. The population would be able to return.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why did you [Audio recording missing], you and your forces [Audio recording missing] them out in the first place? That's ethnic cleansing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you have proof, Mr. Tucker, in cases where you were present in Podrinje Cerska, that we drove them out?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In south-west of Banja Luka and in the eastern enclaves. In other words, Srebrenica, Zepa, Gorazde.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We will come to that. Let us see if that was so, because in your documents it says something different. On page 49 of this document, you say that you -- that I gave my approval for the local police to escort --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at the next page please, and can we look at the bottom of the page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please read this part here, "Agreed to get." What you got from me at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The heading is "Convey to Srebrenica. Srebrenica to Belgrade some help to Skelani," which is on the Bosnian Serb side. "If reported that help goes simultaneously to Serbs as to Srebrenica." Then General Morillon agreed to get the convoy escorted by local police and to arrange its -- and then there's a route Zvornik, Bratunac, Srebrenica and Skelani, and back. Serbs give escort from Zvornik on Saturday or Monday.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we now look at -- yes, I'm sorry. Excuse me. It's not that document. Can we just -- actually, can we just tender this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we add this part to the previous Exhibit D2 -- 2026? Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. I --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, can we get one more page now, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please interpret this paragraph marked with 9, Mr. Tucker. Mr. Tucker, with all due respect, your handwriting resembles the handwriting of a doctor.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. I blame my spider. "Discussion over lunch. Muslims must recognise they will never be allowed to dominate in Bosnia-Herzegovina."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you following the current developments in Bosnia and Herzegovina? Have you noticed that for the past 15 or 16 months there has been no government because the Christian majority, Serbs and Croats, are not accepting Muslim domination?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I've not been following events in Bosnia, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we now look at 65 ter 08561. If nothing has changed, this should be an associated exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That's right. It's P4216.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember this? This is from the 20th of November. It's a report about this meeting with Karadzic and the commander; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I drafted the -- the UN report for General Morillon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. And it can be seen here that I was concerned because of the open intervention of the Army of the Republic of Croatia in Bosnia; is that right? This was also the same that was noted in the handwriting, but if we can look at page 7, paragraph 9, please, now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It has only four pages.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it's on page 3. Not 7, page 3. Evidently it's -- there's something wrong with my articulation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 9. Could you please look at this for us.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That paragraph is consistent with the previous handwritten notes from the meeting itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [In English] And I'll read the rest in English. "Providing the Muslims gave up their claims to rule over all of BH, they could quite happily live alongside each other, but each with their own administration and safeguards for minorities."

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is indeed what was said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Would you agree that it can be concluded on the basis of this paragraph that there would be minorities in the cantons and that they would be protected, that there would be instruments for the protection of their rights?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is indeed what you said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we now look at 1D4862. That's the diary again, and it's page 96. Do you agree that the cantons were not meant to be ethnically pure and that there would be instruments for the protection of minority rights?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's certainly -- can it be enlarged, please. I'm looking for anything about cantons and minority rights on this section but can't see any.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I apologise. I apologise. It's my fault. I put the question that actually relates to the previous paragraph while you were waiting for the uploading. It was in the conversation about cantons and so on and so forth. Did you know that many international authorities stated that a mistake had been made in having secessions take place before putting in place the mechanisms for the protection of minority rights?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not in a position to comment what international authorities may or may not have said, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we look at page 3 of this document. Do you agree that you wrote down here, and you can interpret that for us, that I made efforts through the media to present the neutrality of the UNPROFOR so that we would not have problems when passing through Serb territory?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is indeed what you said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you know that in the media I stated this before and after this meeting and that I would make the statements that UNPROFOR should be trusted?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall specifically for this meeting, but I do know that -- I do recall that on occasions you did make such statements in the Bosnian Serb media. Whether it was immediately before and after this particular meeting, I'm not in a position to confirm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does this then tell you that it's not easy to control civilians and that this was a way of improving their attitude towards UNPROFOR and international organisations?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we look at the place in the next one where you say that I was in favour of securing the -- this is the third paragraph, "Cannot accept." Could you please interpret that paragraph for us?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Cannot accept a long-term grinding on of the war. Want full solution. Cease-fire means can regroup and restart. Cessation of hostilities should lead towards peace." And this is [Realtime transcript read in error "isn't"] in the context of the discussion yesterday about the Bosnian Serbs wanting a cessation of hostilities across all of Bosnia-Herzegovina, whereas the Bosnian Presidency stated they wanted a cessation of hostilities -- they stated they wanted a cease-fire, but they were reluctant to accept the status quo which had been forced upon them through military means and therefore would carry out local attacks and would use cease-fires as a means of regrouping and rearming and replenishing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't think the transcript reflects what you read. Could you read it again for the benefit.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The transcript says "This isn't in the context..." it should read "This is in the context..."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, the quote from your diary above that. The regroup and restart of --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The -- what I can -- cannot accept that -- I start again. "Cannot accept long-term grinding on of the war. Want a full solution. Cease-fire means they can regroup and restart. A cessation of hostilities should lead towards peace."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On several occasions in documents and in reports as well as in the amalgamated statement you said how the Muslims were interested in intermittent and local cease-fires while the Serbs were for a cessation of hostilities and a comprehensive cease-fire and political solution. However, your understanding was that the Serbs wanted to keep everything that they were in control of at that particular time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And were you informed that from the beginning of the war and from the London Conference stated clearly that we were going to return even up to 20 per cent of the territory and that the territorial issues should not be resolved by military means but by means of negotiations?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of what was said in detail at the London Conference. What I do know is that your forces were carrying out military operations in order to seize more territory which -- by military means.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: With the goal of keeping them; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: What the goal of -- was, I'm not in a position to comment. What I can say is your forces were seizing territory and at no time while I was in Bosnia did your forces ever return any territory or allow minorities back in who had been ethnically cleansed by pushing them out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I would kindly ask you to stick to what you know precisely. The minorities returned to Bijeljina before their time, in July and August, and there was a problem. There was killing and chaos. But you don't know that. What I'm asking you this is: Do you know what the objective of the war was for the Muslim side and what it was for the Serb side?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our understanding of the objectives of the Bosnian Serb side was the establishment of an independent Republika Srpska, and it was you yourself and General Mladic who informed General Morillon about that at the first meeting that we had with you in -- with General Mladic in the end of October and I think with you something like the 15th of November when you described in detail what your objectives were. My understanding of the objectives of the Bosnian Presidency was to re-establish the territorial integrity of Bosnia-Herzegovina as the single state recognised by the international community earlier that year.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. Did you know then that this objective of ours, to govern our own part of Bosnia-Herzegovina, had been established and proposed by the European Community before the war and that all three parties had accepted that agreement, and then the Muslim side simply withdraw from it?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not in a position to comment about negotiations and diplomatic matters which happened before I arrived in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But this is what I'm trying to say. If you say that we wanted independence, we wanted an autonomous Republika Srpska within Bosnia-Herzegovina. Did we get that in Dayton? I have to link this up with the situation before the war, because that could have been achieved without a war. Do you agree? We wanted to have an entity of our own within Bosnia-Herzegovina, right?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I can confirm is that at those meetings in October/November 1992, that you and General Mladic and Professor Koljevic described your desires to establish Republika Srpska as an independent autonomy. What I cannot confirm is the other comments you're making about Dayton. You'll need to speak with other people about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But I have to ask you about what had happened before the war, because you are referring to it as if it just came out out of the blue, but do you know this is something that had been offered to us? Do you know that we conceded to an independent Bosnia only on that condition?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I say again I'm afraid, Dr. Karadzic, negotiations and discussions which were conducted before the war, before my time, I did not follow those, and it would be improper for me here to comment about things that I don't know about in detail. I don't know what was or was not said. What I do know is following the media, that many things were said and many positions were taken. What exactly the detail was, I'm not here able today to provide any confirmation or denial.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [In English] Fair enough. Fair enough. [Interpretation] Then we have to look at your general conclusions within that light, that you simply didn't know about this. Is that right? That was my question, and the transcript doesn't seem to reflect it.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, what is the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I said that that was all right, the fact that you didn't know about these things. However, then if we look at your general comments and opinions as to what the Serbs wanted, all of them should be viewed in that light, namely that you did not know about the political processes that had been going on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Witness has made it clear what he knows and what he doesn't know. Move on to your next question, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On this page, could you please take a look. What does it say here, that convoys [In English] Accept -- uh-huh. I cannot -- okay. "We will always give guarantees for the humanitarian aid." [Interpretation] Is that right? And that problems with Srebrenica are temporary and that I asked for patience until solutions are found; right?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you want me to read out the paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, please. You will do it better.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Dr. Karadzic said we will always give guarantees for humanitarian aims. Problems like in Srebrenica are temporary. Please be patient as we need time to organise and prepare our own people."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. This will be added to Exhibit D2026.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: D539. Could we call that up, please. Did you notice that I said that we confirm the rights of Serbs, Croats, and Muslims to freedom, self-determination, safety and security, and so on. Can we have the first page first so that the witness can identify it, and then I'd like to have page 2 displayed. Are you familiar with this document?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's another document that I drafted for General Morillon after attending a meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Towards the bottom it says that this is a personal assessment of the situation, and [In English] "Dr. Karadzic wanted negotiations for peace to be successful. It would be crucial that his forces did not retaliate for the provocations which could continue for some while. Heavy retaliation would be exactly what the radical faction is trying to provoke."

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Provoke.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And that passage is at paragraph 75 of the witness's amalgamated statement.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So you were fully aware of the fact that it had to do with action and reaction and that radical elements on the Muslim side wanted precisely that, Serb responses; right?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That certainly happened from time to time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we have the next page, please. Let us look at 5(a). There's no need for me to read all of it. This is a private conversation, a discussion. And do you agree that you wrote down here that I reaffirmed the right of all Serbs, Croats, and Muslims to freedom, self-determination, and security and so on, that I complained about the lack of confidence and trust? Do you remember that? Do you remember that that had been discussed?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I remember writing that down, but it was because General Morillon told me that that is what his discussion with you had been, because it was a private discussion between yourself and General Morillon. But General Morillon told me that, and I drafted up the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we look at the bottom of the page where there's a reference to the convoy for Srebrenica. You say here, don't you, that this conversation was interrupted often because Mladic, Zarkovic, and Karadzic kept going in and out. Can I have the next page. And this had to do with the progress of the Srebrenica convoy. Do you remember this?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that you had noted here that I and even Mladic were frustrated and even angry because this convoy was not progressing properly?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. [In English] Karadzic apologised for having personally misappreciated the strength of the genuine -- of genuine local bitterness towards the Muslims but hoped they were now being genuinely convinced it was in all people's interest to let the convoys and future ones pass."

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember the words you've just read. I can't see them on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: (D), lower down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it now. Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And further down in paragraph 9 it says that we apologised for the fact that we have not persuaded parliament yet to have additional forces of the Canadian Battalion deployed; right?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is what was said at the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Again, we can see from this paragraph that we had informed you of the intelligence that we had to the effect that Muslim underground movements were waiting just for that, for the arrival of international forces to start an uprising in Banja Luka. We informed you about that. And then on another occasion I'm going to show these documents to the Trial Chamber. However, this is what you wrote down yourself; right?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we have the next page. (F), please. Subparagraph (f) says, isn't that right, that Mladic ordered the arrest of the commander of this Serb check-point and so on; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And these observations --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Sorry, just to be clear, what's correct, that the document says that or that General Mladic ordered that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is correct that General Mladic said that he would order the immediate arrest of the Serb check-point commander, et cetera. I have no knowledge whether that actually happened or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But in paragraph 11, we see your remarks that the meeting was workman-like, devoid of rhetoric, and on the next page you say it was constructive too; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was indeed the assessment General Morillon had after that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And then in subparagraph (c) and (d), we see this observation that it is our true wish to see the convoys get through and that the UN should be taken seriously and then the recommendation to the effect that the Bosnian Serbs were truly interested in seeing progress; right?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I confirm that that is what was said at the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was that General Morillon's opinion? And yours, too, probably, these observations and these recommendations?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were General Morillon's observations, because I drafted these reports up for General Morillon who then corrected and amended them and then signed them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You also wrote about our meeting on the 25th of December, 1992; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And then in 65 ter 11421, page 6, paragraph 3, you confirmed that I gave my consent to have a deblockade of Sarajevo by establishing three supply routes; right?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That's P4220.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct. The document I'm looking at I drafted for General Morillon after the meeting on the 25th of December.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we see 1D4683 now to see what you wrote down in your diary. You can recognise your own diary, can you not? It says the 25th of December, 1992, Pale up here, and then we can take a look at page 3.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I confirm that's my diary.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The upper third, could that be zoomed in. Karadzic agreed three routes: Zenica, Pale, Mostar; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Karadzic agreed three routes. The arrow means from Sarajevo to Zenica, to Pale, and to Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you interpret the rest for us, what Karadzic said, what Morillon said?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Mladic then said: "We need to sit together to agree this." Dr. Karadzic then said: "Ready to meet at Karadzic, Koljevic, Mladic level. No secret meetings." It was Mladic -- General Mladic who insisted -- who made the point about the meeting needed to be open rather than secret. And then General Morillon said: "If you insist on inspecting yourself," what that means is inspecting people who actually go up and down these routes, searching them, et cetera, "then you will be accused of restricting freedom of movements. There is a struggle for power between Izetbegovic and Akmadzic. Akmadzic claimed that Izetbegovic is no longer legitimately hanging on to power. Akmadzic seems determined to --" can you enlarge it. "Akmadzic seems determined to cease the illegality as soon as possible. He said he wants to place -- he wants to place the army under the Ministry of Defence. This is very interesting."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. Do we agree that Akmadzic was a high ranking Croat official and the Secretary-General of Izetbegovic's Presidency?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember the exact appointment that he had, but I do remember that he was a senior Croat in the government of the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What he says seems to suggest that Izetbegovic is not really authorise to hold the position of president of the Presidency because his mandate had not been renewed properly; right?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember the exact details of Akmadzic's assertion, but it was something along those lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. This will be added also to Exhibit D2026.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We also met on the 16th -- or, rather -- oh, yes. I seem to have been there. The 16th of February. We met then, did we not?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And you speak about that in your amalgamated statement in paragraph 133 and then in paragraph 135; right?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is the -- if I recall correctly, the first time that General Morillon met with you since December, because you were in -- you'd been in New York, I believe, in the interim.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I was in New York after that as well, was I not, attending negotiations?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You wrote that down in these two paragraphs and it's also contained in associate exhibit 65 ter 08576. Please, can you confirm that I said that the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina was carrying out attacks in Srebrenica, Bratunac, and that by then 1.260 Bosnian Serb civilians had been killed?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is what you said at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you also agree that I indicated that a mass grave had been discovered, one with 50 bodies, you say, and we said that there were about 50 graves, and the biggest one contained the bodies of 50 Serbs who had been killed while this territory was under Muslim control.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we briefly take a look at 65 ter 08576. Ah, yes. 4228 is its P number. Could it please be enlarged. So the general says this was the first meeting with me since the 25th of December, and I that I said that I would probably not return to York since we were not being treated properly since we had restricted movement. I think that you remember that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please take a look at this. Karadzic stated that the army had carried out a major offensive in Bratunac, Srebrenica, and that at least 1.260 civilians had been killed until then. Do you know that until July 1995, until the end of the war, the Muslim army killed an additional 2.300 Serbs? So that would total 3.500-something civilians in this so-called Podrinje, Zvornik, Bratunac, and so on?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only confirm that you, Dr. Karadzic, stated that 1.260 were killed in that area as written down in this report. I cannot confirm the second figure that you mention.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we have the next page. I'm informing you that Cajnice is under attack, co-ordinated attack. I speak about the discovery of this mass grave. Trebinje is under attack and so on. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we now take a look at what you say about this in your diary. That is 1D4684. Page 335. Do you see this? "Dr. Karadzic, Pale." And now is this General Morillon speaking about Izetbegovic's interview on TV, right?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Morillon described Izetbegovic's TV interview yesterday in which he accepted that the Vance-Owen Plan, be it modified, is the only way forward.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And then further down you see this figure of 1.260 Serbs killed in Bratunac since the 28th of January. Can you interpret this for us. (K).

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Dr. Karadzic said that 1.260 civilians -- Serb civilians had been killed in Srebrenica and Bratunac area since the 28th of January. He has given the strongest order to his local commanders to let UN forces and humanitarian convoys pass. The Muslims are taking military advantage of the convoys and are following up behind them of when they leave the enclaves." I can confirm that is what you stated at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we have the next page now. The fourth paragraph from the top down. It says -- well, can you read it out. Now towards the -- what we see now, at the very beginning. It's at the top of the page now.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't see that yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: (K) and then the first line that you can see on your screen now.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says "Heavy weaponry. Consider the military paper."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And what does it say here?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: After that: "Experience with Muslim and Croats is that they ask for local cease-fire when they are weak and then attack when reinforced. We need a global cease-fire. If they attack Trebinje, we will take Travnik." For clarification, Trebinje was in the bottom right-hand corner and was attacked by the Croats, not by the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Travnik was at that time also controlled by the Croats; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the two major military issues which were being faced at that time by the Bosnian Serbs was the attacks by the Croatian Army from the area of Dubrovnik towards Trebinje and attacks by the Croatian Army across the Sava River and into what was called, at least by the United Nations, the Orasje pocket, out of which they were attacking the Bosnian Serb lines of communication from the east, from Serbia proper, through to the Krajina, and those were the two issues which were of greater concern to General Mladic throughout the time that I was in Bosnia from October 1992 through to March 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I would like to tender this. I'm sorry, did you want to say something else?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: These two military attacks were where the majority of the Bosnian Serb military forces were positioned, and they had relatively limited military sources -- resources available for operations elsewhere within Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. This will be also added to D2026.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When you said the Croatian Army, you were not thinking of the army of the Bosnian Croats but the army of the Republic of Croatia about whose presence we constantly warned?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm looking at the time, Excellencies. Oh, no, excuse me. We have a new schedule. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, the question now is that of Cerska, and I would just like to ask you to recall all the events around Cerska. Do you remember that there was a lot of publicity about Cerska with news reports about an alleged massacre of civilians there in Cerska?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. There were allegations that numbers of Muslims had been shut up in a house or in houses by Bosnian Serbs and that the houses had then been put on fire and that the people inside the house or houses had been burnt to death.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we look at 1D4836, please. Do you agree that Izetbegovic informed General Morillon about these misdeeds and that they were committed by Serbs, that Izetbegovic reported this directly to General Morillon? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not completely correct. What's general -- what President Izetbegovic told General Morillon was that the situation in Kamenica, Cerska, Srebrenica, Zepa, and Gorazde was very bad, that there was no food, that people were dying of starvation, that there were no medicines, that there were reports of atrocities, but President Izetbegovic did not make the information to General Morillon about the people dying in -- being burnt in houses. It was the Muslim commander at Tuzla airport who told General Morillon that people had been burnt in houses and specifically asked General Morillon to when he -- if he succeeded in getting into Cerska to look and see if he could find any evidence. He also said that the Serbs would not allow General Morillon to go and look. When General Morillon met with Naser Oric on the evening of the 5th of March, 1992, Naser Oric also made the same allegation to General Morillon that he had reports of Muslims having been burnt in houses and atrocities having taken place in Cerska.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And you testified to this. We don't have to read any further. You testified about that in this case; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And what you have just talked about now is something that you described in paragraph 160 of the amalgamated statement, and then in 161, 162, these paragraphs, going to 165, deal with that information, dramatic information relating to Cerska; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And let's look at what your diary says about this. This is 1D4685 now. Can we look at the next page, please. Could you please tell us, this one line but last where it says "Cerska," can you tell us about that?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says Cerska 1.500 wounded, 18.000 civilians. And that was information received from Ganic, the -- I think he was the vice-president or something of the Bosnian Presidency, and it was information provided by Ganic at 1550 hours that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the Serbian somebody wrote "Drop aid by parachute, Sokolac;" is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is General Mladic's writing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you kindly read that line again in order to reflect in the transcript correctly, "1.500 wounded," comma, and?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And 18.000 civilians.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Means there are 18.000 civilians?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it means that Ganic claims that there were 1.500 wounded and 18.000 civilians there. Whether that was the reality, obviously we did not know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll take a break. We'll add this part to the previous D2026 as well. We will resume at 20 past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I should like to go through the things that are not in dispute as quickly as possible. Could we please see if General Morillon had gone to Cerska and seen for himself that in Cerska there was no trace of any killing or even fighting, let alone a massacre.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not entirely correct. When General Morillon went to Cerska, what he found was a village where there had been heavy fighting. There's a lot of damage to buildings, but he could not find in the buildings any evidence that buildings had been put on fire with occupant people inside them and people burnt to death. What General Morillon was not able to do was to go out into the woods and the area around the houses themselves to see if anything had happened in the woods.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But nobody ever said something had happened there. The claim was that something had happened in Cerska itself.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your amalgamated statement, paragraph 161, you stated that reports about a large number of civilians being burned alive in their own houses, a claim you repeated in the Oric case, was followed by reports that it was an incident involving 1.500 victims. In fact, in the Oric case, you said that Oric had not been in Cerska, but General Morillon, when he arrived on the 6th of March, found no visible trace of burning of houses or a massacre. That's paragraph 161 of your amalgamated statement; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's 161 through to 16 --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thus not even houses were burnt down, let alone any civilians being burnt down with it?

There were some houses which had suffered fire damage. There were many more houses that had suffered battled field damage, as in shells, bullets, et cetera, hitting them and damaging the houses. But there were no houses of which had been burnt down with people inside them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you accompany General Morillon in that visit?
No. I was back in Konjevic Polje. General Morillon went up into the village and then came back down and briefed me what he had seen, and that is then what I put in the reports that I drafted for him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it true, as you stated in your statement of 2002 and in the associated exhibit 08580, paragraph 11, when you confirmed that the Serbs had allowed General Morillon free access to Cerska, informed him that there had been heavy fighting, and that they had already evacuated Muslim wounded to a hospital, those people who were wounded in battle.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, could we have a reference to at least the page in the 2002 statement, please?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, then I'm wasting time. It's a problem for me. 1D4967, please. Let's call it up. In the associated exhibit it's paragraph 11. Could we see 1D4967 first. It's a statement dated 1 November 2002. Page 8.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I confirm that that page provides more detail about what is referred to in paragraphs 161 to 164.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I can't find it here, but I just rephrased. Is it written somewhere that he got free access and also he returned and found about 30 soldiers from a Serbian platoon who were surprised to see him again?
Yes. I remember writing that, but I can't remember in which document it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And you also confirmed that Larry Bollingworth [as interpreted] was in Srebrenica and returned.
Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It's Larry Hollingworth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we now look at this: Is it true that in your evidence in the Perisic trial -- in fact, it's an exhibit from Perisic. 1D4675. Can we have that? Paragraph 2(B).
It's on the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Towards the top. Let's first make sure. Is it your document?

No. This is a document written by the -- it looks as if it's a UK national documents. You need to go to the first page to the top to see. Yes. It's a report by the UK national command in -- in Salisbury, and my assumption is that it is compiled based on the receipt of reports from the United Nations and from their own people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Hollingworth confirmed that this situation was not as grave as it had been portrayed before. There was no sign of a massacre, there were no cases of undernourishment, and even a few cases of fuel could be found here and there.
That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And under (C), it says that one doctor of the World Health Organisation had stated that there were 200 wounded in Srebrenica; correct?
I can't see paragraph (C).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's go to the second page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that. There needs to be some context behind this. Dr. Mardel, the WHO doctor who accompanied General Morillon into Konjevic Polje, he stayed in Konjevic Polje while General Morillon went up to the village of Cerska in order to assess the injured in Konjevic Polje. This is the context that Izetbegovic had said that there were about 700 injured in Konjevic Polje who needed to be evacuated. Dr. Mardel went around all the houses in the village of Konjevic Polje and only found about 70, I think it might have been 72, rather than 700. So one of the statements that the situation was not as grave as had been portrayed was that there were 72 severely injured, not 700 severely injured. But 72 severely injured is still an issue. His -- Dr. Mardel's statement that there were 200 wounded in Srebrenica is not because Dr. Mardel had yet been to Srebrenica. It was what he was told by -- by Muslims in Konjevic Polje. Dr. Mardel then walked on foot from Konjevic Polje to Srebrenica while General Morillon left the Konjevic Polje area. And when General Morillon arrived back in -- sorry, in Srebrenica for the first time around the 11th, 12th of March, he found Dr. Mardel in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Could we just briefly -- in fact may I tender this document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. This will be next Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 2027, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we take a brief look at 65 ter 08580. It must also have a P number.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Page 3, please, paragraphs 11 and 12. Does it read that Cerska was deserted, apart from a handful of Serb soldiers who had not been expecting General Morillon, and it took an hour of negotiation until the more intelligent local commander turned up, et cetera? Could you present to us this paragraph, please?

Yes. This is a report which I drafted for General Morillon, and the paragraph about General Morillon's visit to Cerska itself was based on information that General Morillon gave me because obviously I had not personally been in Cerska. The -- the situation in Cerska was that Cerska had been captured by the Bosnian Serb forces and that all the people who could move, who could walk, they had already fled from Cerska to Konjevic Polje, and Naser Oric told General Morillon that those refugees had already left Konjevic Polje on foot towards Srebrenica, and when General Morillon arrived in Srebrenica five, six days later, that was when the mass of refugees who had come from Kamenica, from Cerska, from Konjevic Polje, were arriving in -- in Srebrenica because it's quite a long distance to walk in winter through the -- through the hills and the mountains. You will recall yesterday I used the analogy of a broom sweeping dust in front of it. These were in many cases refugees who had in many cases been pushed out on multiple occasions and were on their fourth, fifth, or sixth time of escaping in front of the attacking Bosnian Serb forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please look at paragraph 12 as well. He discusses the same thing. Some houses were undamaged with only windows damaged. Some houses were intact or only slightly damaged, and there was no sign of anything that had been earlier reported; correct?

The -- this report describes what General Morillon told me. It was an area which had suffered one major attack and had been fought over heavily, unlike the areas around Sarajevo which had been fought over for months and had suffered quite a lot heavier damage than these houses in Cerska.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we see the one page but last. Do you agree that you had been informed, and maybe you even witnessed, the Muslim side, especially Colonel Sadic, being indignant and felt let down because General Morillon did not confirm the version that had been put out for the public about Cerska. That's the Tuzla response paragraph.

I -- confirm that -- I confirm that when General Morillon came out of Konjevic Polje and went to Tuzla on his way back to report to President Izetbegovic in Sarajevo, that he met with the commander of the Bosnian forces at Tuzla airport and that they were very angry, and [Microphone not activated] saying that General Morillon was either deliberately concealing the truth or that he had been duped by the Bosnian Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could we see the last page just to take a look at the map, because we're going to show a similar one. Did you or any of your men draw this map of the territory controlled by the Muslims at that point in time, from Konjevic Polje via Srebrenica to Zepa?
That is my map. I drew it by hand. There's a trace over the top of a 50.000 scale map.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me ask you now, Mr. Tucker. You said a moment ago those people had been expelled. The Defence has to get a clarification what you imply by that. It's clear that those people had not been in contact with the Serb army. They had left earlier. They fled earlier. Does fleeing from war something that you think of equal to expulsion?

No. In -- in my own mind, fleeing from war is fleeing ahead of the actual fighting. Being expelled, in my mind, is when you are in your house and somebody physically comes and tells you to get out of your house, you've got 20 minutes to go, and if you don't go there's a strong threat that you will be harmed, and often it happens that in order to encourage you to leave quickly, your house is put on fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did that happen in Cerska, or did civilians leave before the fighters came?

I was -- I was not personally present. I can only report what we were told by refugees who we spoke with, and what they said is that many of them claimed to have been expelled from their houses in towns and villages to the -- to the west and to the north and to the south-west and that they had been expelled back in May, June, July, August, and that they had fled on foot and had eventually ended up in Cerska. Now, in Cerska itself our understanding was that there were a small number of people who had weapons with a limited amount of ammunition in the way that I described yesterday, but there were much larger numbers of these refugees who had been expelled in the way that I described earlier. Now, as the Bosnian Serb forces approached and came close and started shelling Cerska with mortars and artillery, that then -- the refugees then fled further toward Konjevic Polje and then eventually towards Srebrenica. This description -- whilst those who had weapons stayed behind in order in defend the place, and they were the ones who were then eventually overcome in the attack. The way that I describe the use of artillery in order to terrorise the population, in order to flee, is exactly what happened in the areas to the south and south-east and south-west of Srebrenica, which I have described elsewhere in testimony, which is that what would happen is that if you were living in a village and the Serbs were a distance away, the first thing that would happen is that the Bosnian Serb would start shelling the village. So they would fire a shell and maybe -- somewhere into the village, and then 40 minutes later another shell, and then an hour later two shells. In other words, it was not a heavy barrage. But to the civilians living there, these shells effectively acted as terrorism and because they knew that the next thing that would happen was in one, two, or three days then Bosnian Serb ground forces would attack the village, and if they were still there then they were likely to be killed. And so therefore as soon as a village started being shelled, the population then picked up their bags and ran, and it was the people entering Srebrenica from the south, the south-west, the south-east, all fled towards Srebrenica and into Srebrenica because of the -- what I described as terrorism by artillery.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That is precisely what I am challenging in your evidence, Mr. Tucker, that you are making both the indictment and the judgement. I'm not interested in what would have happened in what village. What happened in this specific village? Was Cerska demilitarised? Was it empty of fighters? Did it initiate fighting itself? Was it a civilian area attacked by the Serbs, as you described?
Cerska was a village, a civilian village, into which many refugees had fled, expelled by Bosnian Serb forces. The first point. The second point is that the --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Wait a minute. Wait a minute. Let's see first. Where were they expelled from? Did Serbs expel them or did they flee? If they expelled them, the Serbs, then give us some proof.
What I can tell you is what these people told us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you accept that the warring parties would lie about one another?
In our experience, all three warring parties lied, including your own, Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now, please, do you know what my position was on the issue of civilians in the combat zone regarding Cerska in particular?
I have not heard you make any statements about civilians in the Cerska area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we look at 65 ter 32215. You knew that during the crisis in Podrinje, Cerska, Konjevic Polje, Srebrenica, in 1993, I was in New York; is that correct?
That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we look at the English translation of this, too, please. We do have it. This is my telephone conversation with the prime minister of Republika Srpska, Mr. Lukic. And now I'm going to show you. The first page is not that important. It deals with the negotiations, and I am telling him that this could be accepted but the disputed parts could be protected by the United Nations and the local authority could stay in place. Can we look at page 2, please. And here you can see this one says to me: "I say that perhaps the Russians and British are interested in resolving it that way and that we could accept that." And then Lukic says: "It would be very good, especially because the Muslims, although they are signing it over there, they are not behaving in accordance with that." And I say: "Really?" And then he talks about attacks in Podrinje, Vlasenica, Rogatica, Gorazde. They were all attacking. And then, please, can you look at the bottom, the last line. I say: "Here the newspapers are full of Cerska ..." thinking about this propaganda, about what was going on in Cerska. And can we look at the next page, please. And then he says here that: "It's clear. The papers are full of it. However, our men who went in there found a large number of livestock and farm animals, including some 30 cows, a lot of food. Some even taken from the Serbs," and so on and so forth. Thus it was some sort of a farce in Cerska, you can be sure of it, that there were no civilians there only fighters and that they were mostly feeding their own army. And can you please look at the bottom. [In English] "Certainly not." [Interpretation] I'm asking: [In English] Yes, yes, therefore they are not hungry at all." He said: "Certainly not. They are not hungry." And another important thing: "We agreed to give all the elderly civilians and children a way out in whatever direction they want. "Yes, yes. "Those who want to stay there and live can put down their weapons and there will be no problems. "Karadzic: Yes, yes, I told Mladic to issue a statement tomorrow and that all Muslim civilians may stay where they are or go where they want and -- but armed gangs must put down their weapons." [Interpretation] And can you look at the last one where I say: [In English] "Fine, it would do good for Mladic to issue a statement to that effect tomorrow and to say in the statement that we will give amnesty to all ordinary combatants, that suspected for war criminals would be tried and in accordance with the law, and that the International Tribunal should be present," and so on. This is not propaganda.
