I'm speak with the prime minister, and I'm recommending for him to tell Mladic to give a statement that we will amnesty even the regular fighters and that the civilians may stay. Had you known this, would you have included that in your statement?

What you describe here, Dr. Karadzic, is indeed statements which were made. However, the reality on the ground of what actually happened was rather different. What General Mladic, General Milovanovic, at the meeting on the Yellow Bridge on the 15th of March, et cetera, made very clear is that in practice, all men of combat age, and that was variously described from about 15 up to 60 years of age, would have to be arrested first and would have to be interrogated in order to establish whether or not in your view they had conducted war crimes or not and only then would they be released. That is what in practice in the negotiations was actually said. The second thing to say is that it's one aspect to make claims like this. The reality that the Muslim civilians experienced on the ground was that they were pushed out and there was never any option left for them to stay. When the Bosnian Serb forces came to expel them from their houses, there was no choice for them to stay. When Kamenica was attacked, when Cerska was attacked, there was no choice to stay. Why were they being attacked in the first place?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Sir, we will come to that. Do you believe that when somebody declares war on you that you should not fight, that you do not dare fight? You're a soldier. You know that if somebody attacks you, you have the right to fight, even to capture their capital and to defeat them. Do you have that right?

Fighting soldiers to soldiers, unfortunately happens. What is not acceptable and is against the Geneva Convention is an order to attack civilians. The Muslims in the area of Cerska, Konjevic Polje were not organised military. They did not have chains of command, they did not have military weapons, they did not have equipment. These were people who were attacked and expelled from their houses. Now, if you were attacked and expelled from your house, would you try and defend your house? What these people did was try and seize those weapons that they could get hold of, and I've already described how few weapons they actually had and how little ammunition they actually had. These were not organised military forces. [Overlapping speakers].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] Please, we will come to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, no. Mr. Karadzic, do not interrupt while the witness is answering your question. You put that question. No. No.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was not my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My question was theoretical and academic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I will stop you when you are that obstructive in the future. Please continue, Mr. Tucker.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I've finished.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I kindly ask you to reply to that part of the question that I put to you, because we will go through all of the things that you have mentioned. So you assert that there was no army there, that we were not attacked from that area throughout that whole period, that they did not inflict heavy casualties on us, and that for a year after the start of war for no military reason out of the blue we attacked civilians, entered their homes, and made them leave their homes. We drove them out. Is that what you're saying?

No, it is not entirely what I'm saying. What I'm saying, firstly, is that the people in the Srebrenica enclave were [indiscernible] -- before the war started in April 1992, but were not soldiers, were not in uniform, were not military, were not -- many of them had served as national conscripts in the JNA and therefore knew how to use weapons, but they were not an organised body of -- of force in the same way that the Bosnian Serb Army was. That's the first point I'm making. The second thing is that when those people were attacked, yes, they tried to defend themselves, and they tried to get hold of weapons that they could, ammunition that they could, and they did carry out attacks towards the Bosnian Serb-held areas, and there is testimony that I have given in the Naser Oric case describing how Naser Oric and his men would conduct raids out of the enclaves with the purpose of securing more weapons, and in particular more ammunition, but also food, from Serbs in the area. So, yes, they did carry out attacks going out from the -- from the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So all of your positions, opinions, conclusions that you are bringing forward are based on your knowledge that there was no Muslim army there but that it was a civilian zone; is that correct?

No. These were civilians when the war started. They then organised themselves in order to defend themselves, but there were many, many more unarmed civilians than armed civilians inside the Srebrenica enclave and inside the enclaves. Simply because they didn't have very many weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know what the Patriotic League is, and do you know that it was founded on the 30th of April, 1991?
No, I do not know of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know what Green Berets are?
I know in the context of the British and the US armed forces but not in the Bosnian Serb armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know how many Serbs were killed and expelled before the spring of 1993 from this area that we're talking about, Srebrenica, Konjevic Polje, Cerska, Kamenica, and that whole area?
I've heard various estimates from various sources.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were they expelled by civilians or were they expelled by the Muslim army -- or, rather, the paramilitary going by the name of the Patriotic League?
I cannot comment on Patriotic League. I'm not familiar with the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. You think and you base your assertions on the position that the Muslim armed force in this area did not make war plans and did not implement them before they were attacked in the spring of 1993; is that correct?
No, that is not correct. There were attacks - I will call them raids - conducted by the Muslims in the eastern enclaves prior to the spring of 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. Can we now look at 1D4998. Could we zoom in on this, please. Is this map similar to what you sketched in your own hand? Is that correct?
It is similar. What I don't know from this map is what time is this map meant to represent?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It says at the top April-December 1992. Could we zoom in on that place so that we can see the date and where it says "Map 14." April-December 1992. All right. Can we look at the whole map now so that the witness can see it. Sir, are you asserting that in these two enclaves with Zepa at the time being together with Srebrenica, are you stating that there were no attacks conducted before Serb attacks on their territory? Are you asserting that it was not their assignment to link up with Tuzla through Serbian territory and to liberate this territory?

My understanding is that the Presidency forces in Tuzla and further south in the area of Kalesija and Vogosca were trying to lift the siege of the enclaves. So they were attacking effectively from the west towards the east or north-east. Secondly is that there were infiltration, small groups of people who were trying to carry food and weapons from the main Muslim area into the enclaves in order to help them defend themselves. I also understand that raids were carried out by Muslim forces, armed groups inside the enclaves, out of the enclaves in order to secure weapons, ammunition, food, et cetera, in order to be able to defend themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Sir, how do you know that they were supposed to defend themselves? Who would they be defending themselves from? How do you know that the Serbs did not attack first?

These people were surrounded in the enclaves. They were hungry. They were cut off from the outside world. They had no freedom of movement. There were on occasion Serb attacks towards the enclaves. There is documentary evidence of orders in June/August 1992 and in November 1992 to conduct attacks - this is for the Bosnian Serb Army - to conduct attacks on these -- on these enclaves.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We will show documents. Do you know, sir, that the Serbian side accepted that this remains Muslim territory, and much more than that, and that we issued a proclamation that there was no need for them to fight because in the end there would be a political solution. I personally issued a declaration. Do not fight. There will be no need for that. You will probably end up being in Muslim territory anyway. Do you know about this?
Yes, I remember you making such statements, but your army was issuing orders which were different, and your army was issuing orders which were to attack those enclaves.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And do you know that before that the enclaves were active and they inflicted casualties? They cut off our roads, and even the roads that we were using there were ambushes set and a large number of civilians were getting killed. Did you know that?
Yes, I knew that there were raids being conducted on the Bosnian Serb lines of communication.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you know that other than what you said that they wanted to attack from Kalesija and to deblock the brigades? Entire brigades that were in Kamenica, Cerska, Zepa, and Srebrenica had the same task and the same plans to start moving towards them and to liberate Podrinje from the Serbs, and this is throughout the whole of 1993, orders, plans, actions? Did you know that?

What happened later in 1993 after I left Bosnia at the end of March 1993, obviously I'm not in a position to comment on. What I can say is that there were continued attempts by the Muslims in order to try and relieve the beleaguered population inside the enclave of Srebrenica, Zepa, Gorazde. However, I will also say that the Muslim forces inside the enclaves of Zepa, Gorazde, Kamenica, Cerska, Srebrenica, et cetera, were very weak and that they had very little combat power, and it would be difficult to describe them as an organised military force. I go back to my statements that these were ex-national conscripts who had been attacked and who had picked up the weapons that they could find to defend themselves. They were capable of conducting small raids, but they were not capable of conducting any offensives, any military offensives in order to seize large amounts of ground or anything like that. These were people who were beleaguered and under siege.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And in what way was the Serbian Army different from them?

The Serbian Army was carrying out initially limited attacks. Towards the end of 1992, the Serb -- Bosnian Serb Army was conducting limited attacks towards the enclaves, and the reason for that was that the main threat to the Bosnian Serb existence was the attacks by the Croatian Army in Trebinje and the Orasje pocket, and that is where the Bosnian Serb Army concentrated the majority of their combat power. So they had less combat power to exercise against these enclaves. The Bosnian Serb Army, however, despite the statements that Dr. Karadzic has -- has described making, the Bosnian Serb Army continually had orders and was executing orders to attack and remove the eastern enclaves and those attacks were not that successful in October, November, December 1992, but that in January they re-issued orders in order to close the enclaves, and I saw in Major Pandurevic's office in -- it was about the 18th or 19th of March, I saw on the wall in his office a military map which showed the advances being made by the Bosnian Serb forces around the Srebrenica enclave, showing one line describing the situation on the 7th of February, another line on say the 13th, and another line on -- in order that it showed the way that the -- the attacks were progressing. In other words, there was a deliberate and planned military attempt in order to capture the Srebrenica pocket.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Sir, if you state that, would that imply that you reviewed all the military documents of both sides and established what were the plans on one side and the other side and then established what came first and what followed, what was the cause and what was the effect? Or was it just because you had the map on the wall and came to these conclusions because you spoke with Muslim refugees?
This comes in two steps. The first step is what I knew at the time in 1992, 1993 --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Wait, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Again, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that case I'm asking for enough time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No. You are just arguing with the witness. Please continue, Mr. Tucker.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My knowledge came in two steps. The first step was whilst I was in present in Bosnia in 1992, 1993. What we witnessed was the Bosnian Serbs struggling heavily with the attacks by the Croats in Trebinje and Orasje and not having much combat power to deploy against the Srebrenica pocket, but they had -- then when I saw the map in Major Pandurevic's office, then I became clear in my own mind that this was a deliberate, planned attacked. After the war, I was shown documents from the Bosnian Serb Army during proofing in the preparation for these meetings where I was shown documents and orders from the -- in the Bosnian Serb Army, some from General Mladic and some from the commander of the corps which was based in and around Zvornik and some from Major Pandurevic, and it is from those documents that I make the statements that there were Serb orders and intent to capture the pocket. At the time when I was serving in Bosnia, I obviously did not have that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, let me conclude then that what you are saying does not from your immediate knowledge in the field but from preparation that you had through the OTP; is that correct?
That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did the OTP also show you Muslim documents from that time, military orders, directives, plans and combat reports about what they did in that area?
I think I was shown a couple, but I couldn't recall which.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If you allow me, I will show you this second -- the other side of the truth. Can this page be admitted, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Are you referring to this map?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, just -- actually, when I go back through the transcript, I see the only thing that Mr. Tucker said about this map was that it was similar to the one attached to one of his associated exhibits. I'm in Your Honour's hands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I also remember that he not specifically rely on this map. He referred to the raids from within the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Quite so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And on that basis I think we can admit it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That being the case, Your Honour, just by way of reference, the map was annexed, so Your Honours know, to an open source report entitled "Balkan Battlegrounds, a Military History of the Yugoslav Conflict," prepared by some analysts of the Central Intelligence Agency. And without any further information with regard to some of the markings on the map, it's obviously uncertain as to what weight we might take from this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Have we not admitted some similar maps earlier on?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: We may have. I'm not sure, but I can find out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes. That will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D2028, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] D1596, please. Could we just leave the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Look at this, Mr. Tucker. On the 10th of July, 1992, the Main Staff of the armed forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina issued an order relating to this zone. "The staff of the Srebrenica armed forces with the forces available shall join up its free territories (the liberated territory with the free territory in the general sector of Zepa village and in the general sector of Konjevic village, Nova Kasaba, Drinjaca)." So Zvornik is mentioned in paragraph 1 as well. Paragraph 2 relates to the armed forces of Zvornik. It says it should link up with Kamenica, attacks on Kamenica-Konjevic Polje axis with a view to joining the two parts. And then it says upon linkage and consolidation of forces, the said forces from Zvornik from Kamenica sector and Snagovo sector shall launch an attack in the direction of Osmaci village, and so on and so forth. Can we see the next page?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second yes Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Tucker may be able to deal with this document but we received no notification of it, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, this is in evidence. This is in evidence. I didn't know that the witness would take this position that civilians were there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you are insisting -- anyway, we have to doubt your ability to represent yourself. You should know that you should give notice of documents that you are going to use in your cross-examination. The fact that it's already in the evidence does not excuse you from notifying the other party.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, what am I supposed to do when a new element emerges, when the witness challenges that it was a military area? I'm hearing for the first time that the witness believed there were no military forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, that's not what the witness said. I will allow you to proceed with this, but what you should have said is an apology for -- to -- to the Prosecution for lack of notice. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I can do that much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But, Mr. Tucker, please --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could Mr. Tucker look at all of this, items 3 and 4 in their entirety, and the signature of Sefer Halilovic, Chief of Staff, that is to say the chief commander of all the armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were you aware of this order dated 10 July 1992 relating to the area we have just seen on the map?

Is this the -- the order which had -- sorry. I am aware that Halilovic publicly proclaimed attacks from the main Muslim areas towards the enclaves in order to relieve them and that General Milovanovic, when he met with General Morillon at the Yellow Bridge on the 15th of March, I believe he then requested that that order to attack be rescinded before the Bosnian Serbs were willing to agree to a cease-fire. If that is the order you're referring to, then, yes, I'm aware of that order, but I have not seen this physical document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: 15th of March, 1993.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tucker, without referring to any difficulties, this is a plan for an offensive and the liberation of all that area and its linking up with the territories they consider as free. This is a plan of the armed forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina covering all the areas at that time. Were you aware that these were their activities at the time? This order was indeed implemented and rather successfully. Not completely successfully, but to a great extent.

I am aware that the Presidency forces tried to conduct operations of the kind that are described in this order. I do not agree that they were very successful. The -- the people inside the pocket, inside the enclave, had very little combat power, as I have repeatedly described, and were not, in our view and understanding - and in anything I have seen or heard - capable of doing more than raids out of the enclave. The only places where there was moderately capable military combat power available was in the main Muslim areas of Tuzla, Kalesija, and Vogosca, because they were not surrounded. There were also many, many civilians and refugees inside the enclave, and the number of armed men was very small compared with the number of refugees and the number of civilians inside those enclaves.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But if I tell you that in that area they had 30.000 men, that is to say in the summer of 1999, soldiers, perhaps not completely equipped with uniforms and boots, but 30.000 fighting men who had had their shooting practice in the JNA and who were trained and had officers who were trained in command and control, what would you say to that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did you say 1999?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's mistake: 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would disagree that the number would be anything like as large as 30.000 fighting men in the enclave, because they simply didn't have that number of weapons. There were much fewer people who had weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Sir, I'm not saying in the enclave, but in this area between Zvornik and Srebrenica. If you don't accept 30.000, how many were you aware of?

I do not have specific knowledge of how many armed men there were between -- in the area between Zvornik and Srebrenica, but I would say that 30.000 is a wild exaggeration. The number was much less than that. And all the evidence of all the fighting that happened there is that if there had been 30.000 there, then the outcome of the fighting there would have been very different from the outcome that actually happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And do you know that Oric's 28th Division, which at the time did not exist, but its units did exist, had lost 2.000 men by June 1992, whereas in July 1995, 10.000 men of that division made it through to Tuzla?

It is very misleading to use the terms "division" and "battalion" and "brigade." The word "division" generally in military parlance means an organised body of men of between 10- and 15.000 men. To claim that Oric had a division of between 10- and 15.000 men is, frankly, ridiculous.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you really think you know better than the commander of UNPROFOR in Srebrenica?
I make no such claim.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I am telling you that the UNPROFOR commander in Srebrenica confirmed precisely what I said, whereas Muslim services reported that by 17 July, 10.000 members of the 28th Division made it through to Tuzla under combat. You were right in saying they did not have enough weapons, but they did wage war in three shifts. One soldier would leave the front line and go on home leave but leave his weapon?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, two things. I'd like to have a reference for what UNPROFOR commander in Srebrenica said. Three things, actually. Perhaps we could place this all in time to assist Mr. Tucker. And I'm just wondering what the relevance is of this as we continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's -- he's only arguing with the witness. There's no question. And then what other witness testifies has no relevance to this witness's evidence. You use them as a matter -- as a factor to assess when assessing the credibility of a witness's evidence in your later submission, but it's not time for you to argue with the witness. You're just wasting your time. Consult with Mr. Robinson, as I indicated several times. And by now you have about more than three hours, and you will have about an hour to conclude your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, I come from a different legal system where I have to establish what the grounds are for certain things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then it is a bad decision to decide to represent yourself. We have Rules of Procedure and heed to the advice you are getting from Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I had not finished stating my position. I am not arguing, but it's very important to me whether the witness was aware of these facts when he made his conclusions. It's very important to me. Now I see he didn't know these things and that's good enough for me, a good answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know, Mr. Tucker, that we were able to take Srebrenica in 1993, and I stopped the fighting and even forbade investigations to be conducted into war crimes.

Yes, it was our military -- it was General Morillon's military assessment that the Bosnian Serbs would have been capable of easily capturing Srebrenica in March 1993 if they had wanted to do so. And I am also aware that -- that you from New York made efforts to prevent the -- or ease the situation in Srebrenica. I am not aware of whether you forbade investigations to be conducted into war crimes. It's simply -- I did not hear anything on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. Could we now call up an exhibit - it's already in evidence - just for you to take a brief look?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In the meantime, have we admitted the intercept we saw between Mr. Karadzic and Lukic when he was in New York?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hope so, but if it's not, I would like to tender it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We will mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D2029, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: One more reason why I'm asking you what our objectives were and what theirs were: Our objective was to defend those territories that we believed should become part of Republika Srpska, whereas their aim was to liberate all of Bosnia-Herzegovina.
I have already answered this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: For esteemed Ms. Edgerton, Mr. Franken, deputy commander of DutchBat, confirmed the existence of a very well-structured 28th Division, and he said they had 4- to 4.500 weapons, rifles and other weapons. And that was after the demilitarisation. Do you know that the military forces of the ABH had that many soldiers and that many weapons in Srebrenica after the demilitarisation?

I believe that the time that you are referring to and Mr. Franken and DutchBat, that was all 1995, which was two years after I was there, and I'm not in a position to make any comments about the situation in 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But in 1995, after demilitarisation, they were supposed to have less weapons, not more.
That is not for me to comment about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could we now glance at D00105. While we're waiting, Mr. Tucker, were you able to see for yourself the efforts of civilian authorities and myself to provide unhindered passage to the convoys?

Yes, I was, and the result was that in areas where it wasn't that important, convoys got through, but in areas where people were suffering badly, very few convoys got through, hardly any. It was convenient you -- as was described in testimony earlier today, you made a lot of effort to help get a convoy through to Srebrenica in the end of November 1992. However, the next convoy that got into Srebrenica didn't get through to Srebrenica until March 18 of 1993, and there were many, many convoys which were -- tried to get through but did not get through.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So you believe those areas were more or less important. Do you see any connection between situations where there is military action from a certain area against us and where is not? Izetbegovic said the combat affected areas cannot get convoys until the fighting ends, and is it connected to the fighting in any way?

There is a difference between fighting against organised military forces and starving people and preventing medicines getting through to people who are suffering in grave situations in the midst of a very cold winter up in the mountains of eastern Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you establish that or are you just parroting what the Muslims told you?

I'm describing what I saw with my own eyes when I was in Konjevic Polje and when I was in Srebrenica. I saw with my own eyes the situation and the condition that the unarmed civilians were having to exist in.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you this: Did you establish that they were starving and that we were stopping them from getting medicine? Did you establish that, and did you know that, for instance, international medical organisations always had enough medication for Srebrenica?

You have asked multiple questions there. I'll deal with them one by one going through the transcript. Did I establish that there were starving people? Yes, I did. I saw them with my own eyes. Did you stop them or did the Bosnian Serb forces stop them from getting medicine and food? Yes, they did, because you prevented many convoys from getting through to Srebrenica. Yes, you did get support getting the convoy through to Srebrenica at the end of November, and then again the convoy in about the 18th -- that got into Srebrenica about the 18th or -- 18th or 19th of March. However, those were drops in the ocean compared with the need that was present with all the refugees who had been forced out of their homes and were living in the most appalling conditions in the middle of winter in the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Sir, do you know how many people there were in Srebrenica who did not have their own little farms and food production, or do you believe that all of the 30.000 population depended solely on humanitarian aid?

There are many estimates which have been made about the number of people in the Srebrenica enclave. It is, to the best of my understanding, but it is based on these various estimates and what I have seen myself, that there were probably something like 40.000 people in the Srebrenica enclave at the -- during -- during March, and that of those 40.000 people, about 7- or 8.000 were actually living in their own houses and thereby had the ability to store food and draw on food which had been stored earlier. The remainder were all refugees who had had to walk from the houses from which they had been expelled or had been force to flee because of terrorism by artillery, as I described earlier, and those people only had what they could carry with them. Generally speaking, when people had to flee from their houses, they tried to carry as much food with them as possible, but that food, as you can imagine, how much food can you carry with you on foot with your own hands. It can probably last five to ten days. Now, many of these people had been on -- on foot fleeing for many months, so of the 40.000 people in Srebrenica, they were having to live off literally the food, the bark they could scrape off trees, biscuits made from a yellow flower which grew on the hills around Srebrenica, and from humanitarian aid. Dr. Karadzic, I ask you, would you risk standing in the middle of a drop zone where pallets weighing about 4- to 500 kilos are being dropped and fight with knives in order to get access to these pallets once they have landed if you had enough to eat?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And who told you about though bread crusts and the rest? Did you check that out?
I saw them myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you see people making bread out of bark? What exactly did you see? Could you describe it?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours. There's just a line missing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I was told by the interpreter. Could you put a bit of distance from the microphones. Thank you. Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Line 3, it wasn't captured. Actually, the witness said, "I saw it myself," in respond to Dr. Karadzic's response about bread crusts and the rest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I confirm hearing that too. Can you confirm it as well, Mr. Tucker?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I saw it myself, and so did everybody who was with General Morillon and me in Srebrenica in March 12 through to March 20 or so. We all saw it. It's even reported -- it's in a medical report. I can't remember if whether it's by Dr. Mardel or by someone else, but I've seen a number of reports. I think Larry Hollingworth also comments on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And who showed you this?
I saw it myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You actually went into a house and saw them making food? Somebody had to show you. If you went into a house, which house did you go into?
I went into many houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And in all those houses they showed you food they were making out of bark; right?
They weren't making food out of bark. They were eating bark. They were making food out of the yellow flowers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Sir, do you know that all their villages were full of intact households that had two cows each, 10 to 30 sheep, and one of the witnesses here confirmed to us that all of them had cattle and food and produced food? Were you aware of that? In Srebrenica you were able to see chicken and even goats. Goats are seen in one video that we have here. And you claim that in such circumstances people would be eating bark.

I cannot confirm your previous statements about intact households, et cetera, et cetera. What I can tell you is what I saw with my own eyes, which is houses with rooms. In each room there were 15, 20 people squeezed together. They could not all lie on the ground at the same time. You must remember that the temperature outside was minus 15, minus 20 degrees. This was the winter. And these people had no food with them. When I was in Srebrenica in -- in March 1993, I did not see any chickens or any -- any cows in Srebrenica. They had already been eaten. There may have been a goat, but I don't think it lasted very long. I can tell you that with my own eyes I saw people who were very thin, people who were starving, children with their bellies swollen out because of lack of food and lack of medicine. I saw people who were so ill from lack of food and lack of vitamins and medication that their eyes had gone all dull and that they could not -- they could barely stand up. Was everybody like that? No. But were people very hungry and were people starving? Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, with respect to Dr. Karadzic's comment that -- to the effect that witness -- witnesses here had confirmed that all of them had cattle and food and produced food, I'd like to see a reference, because I haven't seen a single mention of that in the whole transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let us proceed, yes. Be precise when referring to the previous transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know that the Trial Chamber knows. I think it was a protected witness who told us here all the things that he had.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Be precise. Ms. Edgerton is aware of that. She raised it because you were not precise. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I don't have enough time to show it. I wanted to show whether the witness knew that or not. I don't have to convince him of that today. I want it to be in the transcript --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, you have about half an hour to conclude your cross-examination. It's up to you how to use that remaining time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is immediately after my return from New York. Did you know about this order in which I in a way saved and supported the Main Staff, that it could refer to the fact that they could not undertake any offensives without my approval? Did you know about this order?
No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And do you see that here it is also very strictly stated that convoys have to be allowed to pass unhindered; is that correct?

I'm not in a position to confirm or deny this document. What I can say is that at the meeting with General Mladic on the 26th of March, 1992, that General Mladic agreed to allow humanitarian convoys to pass into -- into Srebrenica and that a convoy then got into Srebrenica on the 28th of March, in other word a couple of days later.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We won't be needing this document any more. Sir, you talked about Sarajevo and what you knew about that, and you also said how you established that there was justified shelling from a military point of view and that there was also punitive shelling; is that correct?
That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you know what the deployment of the forces was in Sarajevo?
I did not personally follow the reports about the deployment of the BiH forces in Sarajevo, but people in Sector Sarajevo did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. And on the basis of what did you state, did you conclude, that Serbian shells were coming from the hills? You said something like that; correct?
The Serbian shells came from the hills because that's where the Serbian guns were located and that is from where I saw and heard Serbian shells being fired.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was the Muslim army also in the hills around Sarajevo, their positions, their mortars, recoilless guns, and so on?

No, the Muslim positions were inside the encircled area, which was mostly in low ground of Sarajevo, except for the high ground up to the north-west of Sarajevo, up towards the television transmission tower.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You're talking about Hum where the TV tower is. Do you know that all around Sarajevo, on all the hills, there were Serb and Muslim positions, the lines lying next to one another?

The lines were obviously next to one another because they were fighting. However, the Muslim lines were on the inside and were lower down the hills than the -- the Bosnian Serb positions, which were higher up, because they were surrounding Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: They were not living around Sarajevo, but they came and surrounded it; is that correct?
If you're talking about the Bosnian Serb soldiers, no, they lived elsewhere, but in their combat positions, they were at the front line around Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You don't know that, sir, either. If I were to tell you that the entire Sarajevo-Romanija Corps was made up of people whose homes were immediately along the front lines, what would you say?

I'm not in a position to -- to state where the -- each individual soldier lived, but I will say that no soldiers were living on the front line, that their houses may have been nearby. That's entirely plausible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When you say that we were not able to or could not take Srebrenica at the time in 1992 because we were under pressure from the Croat army, then did any of the Drina Corps units fight outside of the Drina Corps AOR? Did any of them fight in the Trebinje or the Gorazde area?
I cannot confirm or deny that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I note the time. We'll take a break now for two hours and ten minutes and resume at 10 past 3.00. When you have a -- you will have about 25 minutes to conclude your cross-examination. Oh, I'm corrected. You have half an hour.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I must say that that is not enough for 307 or 308 paragraphs in view of the fact that the witness is very willing to expand and -- his answers and give general statements. I have to contest those general statements. Could you please take into account that a number of OTP witnesses have not been cross-examined. I don't know what weight you are going to attribute to things that are not founded on fact but founded on propaganda, but the Defence cannot take that risk. It would like to confront the witness about the way in which he came to his conclusions and how he came to know what he knows.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, the Chamber is of the opinion that four hours has been allowed for your cross-examination is more than sufficient time, and you cannot argue for further time after having wasted so much of your time for matters not directly related to the indictment and making statements unnecessary and improper. You'll have half an hour after the break. We will resume at 10 past 3.00. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.02 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tucker, could I ask you to take a look at a letter, 1D04850. 1D04850. Could we please have that in e-court?
My screen is switched off.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Neither I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is it on Sanction? It is restarting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While we're waiting, let me say that this has to do with Sarajevo. You spent about four months there, right?
That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I've already asked something. I'm not sure about all the questions I've asked. On the Serb side, there was the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps that had between 15- and 17.000 men, and on the Muslim side there was the 1st Corps of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina that had up to 80.000 men, out of which 40.000 were in the city itself.
I'm not in a position to confirm those figures. There's obviously your information --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness speak closer to the mike. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What was the information you had? How strong was the 1st Corps?
We had difficulties assessing the size of the 1st Corps because the organisation kept on changing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. However -- well, all right. Please take a look at this letter. Do you agree that this is a letter sent to the president of the Presidency -- no, no. No. President -- actually, can we see the bottom, the bottom page. The president of the Security Council, in actual fact. And you'll see ultimately that it's the Secretary-General that's writing this letter. Could you please scroll down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Second page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Down here. I see. On page 2 we see who is writing the letter, Boutros Boutros-Ghali. And now can we go back to the first page. You see this here, the Secretary-General is informing the president of the Security Council about what is going on in Sarajevo around the 9th -- or, rather, 8th of September. In the second paragraph it says that military personnel wearing uniforms of the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina were observed -- actually, there were attacks and people in uniforms of the Bosnian Army are recording that. Isn't that right? That's what it says here. And these were attacks against UN vehicles.
May I say that this attack happened before I arrived in Bosnia, in Sarajevo, and I'm aware in general that it happened, but I don't know any details about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. However, that was close to the time when you arrived. Did you know that the Muslim side was firing at the representatives of the UN and that they had sustained losses, the UN I mean?
Yes, it happened on occasion.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could this please be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D2030, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. 1D04677. Could we have that, please. Again we're in Sarajevo, the 13th of September, 1993 -- or, rather, the 13th of February, 1993. Could we have the next page, please. You were there at the time with General Morillon. Do you see that it says here that Izetbegovic had been informed about the evidence from the fatal mortar attack on the French battalion? That had happened in September, and this happened in February. Please look at the second paragraph where it says that Siber tried to justify this by saying that it was not possible to determine the direction. However, the UN believed that this was an attack by the Muslims; right?

Yes. I was at that meeting. Yes, that is the discussion that had happened at that meeting, which I drafted for -- for General Morillon, and, yes, the technique of crater analysis was used by the United Nations whenever possible to identify the direction and the range from which artillery or mortar shells had been fired.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please take a look at this where it says Eastern Bosnia. General Morillon is writing to UNPROFOR in Zagreb [In English] I particularly emphasise that we had indications that the eastern enclaves had carried out an offensive and were now by all accounts suffering from the Serb counter offensive.
That is indeed what was said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Were you convinced that the Serbs were shooting more than Muslims in the zone of Sarajevo? I'm referring to heavy weaponry.

The Serbs were shooting -- the Bosnian Serbs were using heavy weaponry around Sarajevo rather than more than the BiH Army was for the simple reason that the Bosnian Serb Army had many more artillery guns and much more ammunition than the surrounded forces of the BH Army inside Sarajevo who had very limited arms and ammunition.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But you yourself established that the Muslim army had considerably more personnel and that the Serbs had more weapons and that that was their strategic advantage; right?
That -- that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is what I'd like to ask you now: Did you see the lists referring to the heavy weapons of either side and how much ammunition they spent, and did you see the reports of military observers about incoming and outgoing fire on the Muslim side and on the Serb side?
These are the reports around Sarajevo. Yes, we saw them every night.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we have the next page, please. If I were to say to you that we saw lists here of daily consumption -- of the daily consumption of the 1st Corps in the zone of Sarajevo, and we'll be looking at this even more, and I have to say that although they had less heavy guns, it doesn't mean that they used less ammunition. Look at this, the 11th and 12th of February, 1993. On to Serb territories one thousand -- 144 grenades and on to residency areas 399, and on the 12th of February a bit less, but again the Serbs were hit two times more than the Muslims. Did anyone inform you about that kind of thing that was going on, that the Muslim side was firing as much as the Serb side was and often even more?

That only happened in exceptional situations, was very rare. One other occasion that I'm aware of was when the Muslims tried to break the siege of Sarajevo in the Otes and Stup area around the 7th of December, 1992, but I'm sure that if you look at these reports you will again see that the numbers fired by the Muslims were high, but when you take the entire time that I was in Sarajevo, by far the majority of fire was from the Serbs into the city rather than from the city outwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we see the fifth page. So four pages up, please. The fifth page from here. Do you remember this letter sent to Izetbegovic by Morillon on the 13th of February, 1993, and he is telling him about the results of the investigation into the fatal mortar attack against the French.
Yes, I drafted that letter for General Morillon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we have the next page now. I would kindly ask you to look at the -- [In English] "I must, however, request you to restrain the populations of the enclaves from offensive actions as aid cannot be delivered where your forces are engaging in active hostilities."
Again, that is a letter that I drafted for General Morillon, and I'm aware of the contents.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D2031, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we now briefly take a look at 65 ter 21646. Yes. Please take a look at this. It is your message, and it has to do with your information -- or, rather, your contacts with Oric, and it says: [In English] "The local military commander of Srebrenica received the order from Halilovic to stop any offensive actions towards the -- or against the Serbs. As already stated before, every night some raids were conducted and between 5 and 15 Serbs were killed every night."
That is correct. That is a transcript of a report which I radioed from inside Srebrenica to the headquarters in Kiseljak in Dutch. It's been translated into English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D2032, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we now, since we're in the area, this was March 1993, can we have 1D04833. Let us see how things developed in December 1992. Do you remember a letter I wrote to General Morillon on the 10th of September, 1992?
That was about a month before I arrived, so it's probably unlikely that I saw it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were you not there in the autumn of 1992?
Sorry, you said September. This is December. In December I was indeed there. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Uh-huh. I see. Maybe it's a translation issue, but we do see December written here, so what is described here is one such attack that occurred on the 7th of December when people working in a mine were killed. Eleven were killed and 21 wounded, and it says that they had weapons and ammunition from Arab countries and several UNPROFOR packages. I am asking General Morillon to see whether this had anything to do with the convoy that had just arrived in Srebrenica. And in Cyrillic there is an attachment, a letter written by the municipality of Milici who informed me about what happened, and there is a reference to weapons and ammunition produced by Arab countries, as well as several UNPROFOR packages. Do you remember that I informed General Morillon about this?
Yes, I believe you did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would you like see the translation of the attached letter?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'd like to see the attached letter as well, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we mark it for identification, pending translation.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 2033, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, was that your point, Ms. Edgerton, when you rose?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Maybe it's a technical thing, but what I have doesn't have a Cyrillic letter attached. So that was my point, actually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you have the second page?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we have time I'm going to read it. I'm going to read it carefully so that they --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No. We need a translation by our section. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Also in your statements and in your amalgamated statement, too, I think, you mentioned that you were aware of the abuse of certain buildings in the city itself, there was the Muslim soldiers that were using these buildings to fire from them, like from the hospital. So they had firing positions that were actually impermissible; isn't that right?

What I described was two particular kinds of incident. One was when Bosnian Army units would move mobile mortar -- mortars into the area of the Kosevo Hospital, would then fire their mortars out of Kosevo Hospital in order to try and provoke the Serbs to fire counter-battery back at the position from which the mortars had been fired, and they would -- that incoming fire would therefore land on the -- on the hospital. That's one example. The second example was when Muslim BiH Army units placed mortars next to General Morillon's headquarters and similarly fired out at the Serbs, presumably in the hope that the Serbs would fire counter-battery bombardment in a similar way and would thereby potentially hit the UN headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. 1D01956. Could I have that, please. Also, you noticed, did you not, that there were mobile mortars mounted on trucks? Isn't that right?

I did not personally see them, but a British Army sergeant major who was part of the UN forces who was responsible for delivering diesel fuel to the Kosevo Hospital to power the generators, it is him who saw, and the words that he used was "mortars mounted on the back of trucks." There were other reports we had from other parts of UNPROFOR in Sarajevo who talked about mortars being placed in the back of cars and -- like Volkswagen Golfs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And was the point of that to allow them to move after having fired so that the Serbs would fire into an empty space?
Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we have the next page now. Do you agree -- actually, you probably drafted this too. General Morillon is writing about violations of the Geneva Convention and is describing the incident that you have just described, right?
Yes. I think that's it. I just need to see the next page just to make -- because it talks of attachments.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. Could I have the next page as well, please.
Yeah. That is the incident I was referring to when I just mentioned that a British Army sergeant major reported.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could we briefly take a look at the next page and then the one after that again. That's part of it, isn't it? You know who Cutler is, don't you?
Yes, he was an officer serving with the UN in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could we have the next page now. This has to do with the same incident.
Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now, please, the very last page where General Morillon is writing to the President of the Presidency, Izetbegovic, warning him about these violations of the Geneva Convention. This has to do with that incident and also that particular set of documents; right?
That is correct, and I drafted this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could this set of documents please be admitted under the same number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Exhibit D2034.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You were aware, weren't you, you confirmed that for us anyway, that the parties in the conflict were prepared to deceive the representatives of the UN and lie to them. Is it true that you heard rumours to the effect that the scene that was staged by the Muslim civilians in Konjevic Polje had been orchestrated, that it wasn't actually authentic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D04676. Could the witness please be shown that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Does this relate to the situation in which Muslim civilians blocked you, where two British soldiers were perhaps wounded in Konjevic Polje, or injured, and the mob blocked that location, and the appraisal was that the whole thing was orchestrated, not spontaneous?

No. That is not quite correct. There are two incidents here. The incidents referred to here in Konjevic Polje is when the British Battalion based in Tuzla sent some armoured vehicles into Konjevic Polje and some transport vehicles in order to evacuate injured and wounded, and that was arranged after General Morillon's visit to Konjevic Polje on the 5th and the 6th, and approval was given by the Bosnian Serb authorities in meetings on the 8th and the 9th of March. When the British arrived there, they arrived on the evening, I believe, of the 11th, and when they tried to leave on the 12th, anxious refugees crowded around the British vehicles, and Serb tanks, and infantry fired into the crowd and -- who were clustered around the British vehicles, and a number of civilians were killed and injured two British soldiers. That is one incident. The second incident is - and that's what is referred in paragraph 2 - is in Srebrenica itself, and the crowd blocking this location refers to the crowd blocking the PTT building in Srebrenica. And the crowd surrounding the PTT building in Srebrenica which prevented General Morillon from leaving on the 12th of March, that crowd of refugees was orchestrated. The way it was orchestrated was that there were refugee women with whistles who were walking around the back of the crowd and blowing whistles and giving instructions to the crowd as to where to go and how to block General Morillon and his team, my team, when we tried to get into the vehicles in order to drive away from the PTT building. Now, the crowd that was being orchestrated were not being orchestrated against their will. They were being orchestrated because the crowd were very anxious that if General Morillon left, they believed that then they would be shelled, because on previous occasions when General Morillon had visited somewhere, the Serb shelling and attacks had stopped, but as soon as General Morillon had departed, the Serb shelling and attacks started again. So the -- the crowd of numbers of thousands of refugees who were crowded around the PTT building, they were already very anxious, but they were orchestrated and controlled as well by these women who were taking instructions from the Srebrenica war council. After the war, I heard that the Presidency had apparently given instructions to the Srebrenica war council to try and prevent General Morillon from leaving and that they were executing that and using the crowd in the way that I described.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D2035, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could we now see 1D04678. I believe this is your report, in fact. It says it's your report. 1D04678. It refers to a vicious circle in central and Eastern Bosnia, and you speak about our aspiration to have a cease-fire, an overall cease-fire, beginning with mid-November. Are you familiar with this report?
Yes. That is indeed what -- what I said at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we now see the next page. In fact, the two next pages. The second one is in English, and the third one -- no. In fact, page 3 is the English translation of the French text. This is where General Morillon is reporting to someone. It must have been by radio; correct?

Yes. Remember that we were inside Srebrenica and had no direct contact with the UN headquarters in Kiseljak, and for this particular report General Morillon himself spoke on the radio, and he spoke to Major Olivier de Bavinchove, who is the person I think signed at the bottom who is a French-speaking officer based in Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does it follow from this that after I approved an air corridor between Tuzla and Srebrenica, Morillon asked that your helicopters move information and that Serbs be notified that helicopters flying in formation belonged to the UN, not the Muslims, because a Muslim white helicopter flies alone? Isn't that written here?
That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That will be admitted as Exhibit D2036. And, Mr. Karadzic, I wanted to remind you that your time is up, and it's time for you to conclude.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, I have two or three more documents and I'm not spending much time on them. May I be allowed to finish?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: 65 ter 21647. At that time I was still in York, right? But somebody's contacting me, correct?
That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: 1(a), you are sending a message that I approved the air corridor from Tuzla to Srebrenica for five days and that's the basis upon which Morillon later asked that UN helicopters fly in formation so that Serbs know that it's not the Muslims.

I recall the -- the text which is in this document. The comments about flying in formation, the previous document talks about large formations. What I cannot recall is the exact figures which were actually agreed with the Serbs. The previous letter is -- the previous document is an internal discussion between General Morillon and -- and Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But that was on the basis of my approval, and it follows from that that flights were allowed, but the only problem was that the Muslims had a white painted helicopter; right? That was in the first document.
Yes. The Muslim had a white painted Hip helicopter that I saw at Tuzla airfield.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Exhibit D2037.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have one document now that I should not like to be broadcast, and we don't have to refer to the institution from which it originated, and Ms. Edgerton can intervene. 1D3830. Do we have to go into private session, or can we just not broadcast it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Probably we go to private session. Shall we?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We are now in open session.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it true that you had information that the Muslims were opening fire on their own populous, on their own people? I mean primarily mortality fire.
There were reports in the media that that happened in Sarajevo, but that was after I left Bosnia, and therefore I had no information beyond what was in the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it true that you met in Germany with a British officer who informed you that the shell at Markale Market-place came from Muslim positions?

When I was back in Germany after my time in Bosnia, I met by coincidence a British sergeant major who was a specialist in crater analysis and artillery intelligence who had been on the investigating team looking into what I believe is referred to as the first market-place incident, and he said to me that he believed that that the first market-place incident had been fired or had come from the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, please conclude.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one question and one document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you know that there was a private aeroport for two-winged planes in Bratunac, and what you perhaps saw were those little planes dropping something, but they came not from Serbia but the airfield in Bratunac?

I'm aware that there was a small grass airfield on the outskirts of Bratunac. You are referring to the reports while I was in Srebrenica which was made by two UNMO officers who reported seeing planes fly from over Serbia, across the Drina River, into the air space over Bosnia-Herzegovina, drop some bombs and then fly back. All I can -- I did not see these myself. All I can repeat is the words that those UNMO officers reported and which I include in the reports and which I have certainly give -- testified in previous cases and ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My last question and last document. D43. While we're waiting, and I've mentioned this before, I issued an order to the army to stop before Srebrenica, not to enter, and not to investigate war crimes, to avoid any possibility of revenge or uncontrolled processes that pending defusion of tensions, nothing should be done. I believe we have a translation for this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is the 16th of April, after all the crises and the fighting in Eastern Bosnia. This is my order. Stop the forces at the positions reached and prevent their entry into Srebrenica, facilitate the passage of all humanitarian convoys, ensure pacification of the town in such a way that Muslim forces surrender weapons to UNPROFOR. I underline this: Not to the Serbs but UNPROFOR. And store these weapons on a two-key basis jointly with the Serb forces. After the surrender of weapons, all Muslim soldiers should be treated like other civilians. If you remember my conversation with Lukic, I said that all Muslim fighters should be treated the same as civilians, should be amnestied. Do you remember that intercept I showed?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: This area of questioning has been the subject of other questions by Dr. Karadzic. It's been talked about at length today, but this is a document we haven't been notified on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What is your question, Mr. Karadzic, about this document? That should be your last question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise to Ms. Edgerton, and I promise I will be tolerant whenever they do the same thing with documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree, Mr. Tucker, that what I announced was specification, treatment of fighters as civilians, and what it says in point 6 is: "Do not conduct any investigation into crimes ..." Do you agree what I discussed with Lukic was operationalised through this order and were you aware of this?
The date of this document is the 16th of April, 1993. I left Bosnia at the very end of March 1993. So I cannot confirm the contents of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well this, document is in evidence. I just want to know the extent of your knowledge and what was the basis for your positions. Thank you, Mr. Tucker. May I just ask you one thing? Do you all stand by all of your documents so I can tender them through a bar table motion, the documents that you drafted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No. How can he answer that question without seeing all the documents? Yes, Ms. Edgerton, do you have any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Four minutes, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Sorry, let me switch microphones. Mr. Tucker, you talked at length today with Dr. Karadzic about events in Eastern Bosnia, and I wonder whether you might remember him saying to you at one point, and for the record it's on page 62: "Our objective was to defend those territories that we believed should become part of Republika Srpska, whereas their aim was to liberate all of Bosnia and Herzegovina." And also asking you at line 14 whether you had proof in cases where you were present in Podrinje Cerska that we drove them out. Do you remember those two passages?
Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Then I'd just like to go back very quickly to what's now P4249. It's a document you've seen before and commented on at paragraphs 264 and 265 of your statement. It's an order dated 24 November 1992, from the Drina Corps command to the Zvornik Light Infantry Brigade, and your indulgence for a moment. Now we see the document on the screen in front of us. In that order, in paragraph --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your indulgence for a moment, Your Honour. I might have got the P number wrong. I'll try a 65 ter number. 01900.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By the way, if I may, this is the date three days after the massacre in the bauxite mine. So it would be nice to place things in context.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You can give your evidence. Is it coming?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: My colleague might be able to help me.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one thing. My intonation indicated that "liberate" was in quotation marks. That's a linguistic difference. "To liberate" should be in quotation marks, line 24.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, you are not giving evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's true, Your Excellency, but I see it's not recorded properly. There are no quotation marks.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Pardon me. I was going by an exhibit list I received and I think there might actually be a date issue. Give me one minute, please, and I extend my four minutes I requested.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I think I've got the problem sorted and my sincere apologies, it should be P2085. I'm out of practice, Your Honour. My sincere apologies. P2085.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is it a November document, November 1992?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It is indeed, 24 November 1992. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now to go back to my question. This is the order I was describing before, dated 24 November 1992, from the Drina Corps command directing forces of the Zvornik Light Infantry Brigade to launch an attack using the main body of troops and equipment to inflict on the enemy the highest possible losses, exhaust them, break them up, or force them to surrender and force the Muslim local population to abandon the area of Cerska, Zepa, Srebrenica, and Gorazde. Now, Mr. Tucker, is this what you saw happening on the ground in March of 1993?
The attacks ordered in this document are what I saw and what the whole world saw take place in February and early March 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Then nothing further.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I just say one thing?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, Mr. Karadzic. No Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I said no.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't even say it yet. I am just telling you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. I said no without hearing what you had to say. Mr. Tucker, that concludes your evidence. On behalf of this Chamber, as well as the Tribunal as a whole, I would like to thank you for coming to The Hague again to give it. Now you're free to go. Please have a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Tieger, I note the time, but having asked the next witness to come by, I think we can go with him at least for ten minutes. Is it practicable for you?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It's certainly not a problem for me, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We are going to hear him in closed session. I was advised to take a five-minute break. We will resume at 20 past and go on till half past. --- Break taken at 6.13 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 19th day of January, 2012, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 4.33 p.m.
